tweets.text:
As promised, here’s my setup for cross-channel analytics ↓

https://t.co/dRaWjAst9l

TL;DR:

→ Components

Google Sheets = database: one spreadsheet for content, plus separate spreadsheets for paid placements, zero-cost marketing experiments, and SEO.

Typefully = a list of published posts via API, including full text and tags.

GA4 (+ Search Console) = traffic and sign-ups on the newsletter site, by page and source.

n8n = glue. A workflow runs twice a week, collects new posts from every platform, labels them, and writes snapshots into Sheets.

Claude built most of the above with me: it labels posts, loads the weekly exports, writes the weekly analysis, and builds the dashboard (I also have it as an artefact for visualisation).

Native exports: Substack (subscribers, traffic sources, growth sources), Telegram channel statistics, and X analytics CSVs.

→ The workflow

Twice a week (Monday and Thursday morning), the n8n workflow pulls new posts: the Substack archive and notes, the public web page of the Telegram channel, and published drafts from Typefully. Every new post gets a row.

A model suggests a topic (one of 12 marketing directions, e.g., SEO / SMM / Strategy), a format for newsletter issues, and a post type based on the desired target action—e.g., discovery (main goal: maximise shares) or resource (main goal: link clicks). I review the labels once a week and correct them. Edited copies of the same post on other platforms are detected automatically and inherit the original labels.

At 7 days and 30 days, the workflow writes a metrics row for each post. Public numbers (likes, restacks, views, reactions) come in automatically. Private ones are added by hand from screenshots.

On Monday, I drop the Telegram, X, and Substack exports into a Claude chat. Claude loads them into the right tabs, checks the totals against the files, and writes a short summary of the week.

A single page reads the sheets and shows trends, top posts relative to a typical post on that platform, article promotion windows, and a “this week” to-do list.

Full breakdown → https://t.co/XUkqpncnbR

In 2026, you have to fire your marketer if they:

1. Fully rely on AI to write content for your socials

2. Don’t track how your brand appears in AI search results

3. Launch campaigns because “a competitor did”

4. Build marketing strategies with ChatGPT and don’t verify its claims against real research and data

5. Think “AI influencers” are still a viable growth strat

6. Stop underperforming campaigns without understanding why results were poor

7. Can’t name at least 3 key marketing trends for 2027

8. Can’t attribute traffic spikes to any specific source

9. Have no idea what they can do to improve retention from the marketing side

10. Don’t experiment with AI for customer research, performance tracking, or data analysis

What else?

This might be the most bullish HydroGraph $HGRAF valuation table you’ve ever seen: a long-term scenario showing potential 1,000× upside.

An average selling price of US$500/kg doesn’t strike me as unrealistic. The bigger questions are production scale and the P/E multiple investors would be willing to pay.

But if HydroGraph’s graphene becomes a standard additive across plastics, coatings, cement and automotive applications, could those assumptions eventually be within reach? If we start seeing major contracts from early adopters and their competitors follow suit, the stock will for sure go bonkers imo.

Of course, this is only speculation. I’d be happy with 100× or even 10×, too. Please do your own research.

Thanks, Kevin. Fair points, especially on the sales mix and the additional processing costs for RGA. A higher selling price doesn’t automatically mean proportionately higher margins, and large bulk orders could pull the average closer to the lower end.

That makes $500/kg look ambitious. Perhaps $300/kg is a more sensible modelling assumption, although actual contracts will give us a clearer picture.

I agree that the bigger opportunity is the potential tonnage. Converting evaluators into contracted customers and scaling production at strong margins could still deliver enormous upside with a much more conservative selling price. Better to leave room for positive surprises.

In 10 years as CEO of two startups, I can't count how many times engineers pitched me a complete rewrite of our codebase.

It always reminded me of Steve Blank's Startup Suicide: Rewriting the Code and Joel Spolsky's Things You Should Never Do. Joel compared rewriting software from scratch to demolishing a building instead of renovating it. I always agreed and pushed back hard on rewrites.

But AI has completely changed my mind.

When you can coordinate a swarm of thousands of coding agents, the economics are completely different. Suddenly there's an enormous premium on having an agent-native codebase: super fast CI, minimal dependencies, clean architecture, every decision documented, and everything optimized for agents rather than humans.

For the first time in my career, I'm starting to think a complete rewrite might actually be the right call.
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
The thing with AI:

You REALLY can replace existing software with something that is much faster in performance, much cheaper to operate, as reliable (or more!) as before, with shockingly little effort when you know how to use AI

Expertise has never been this valuable!!

If you're building in AI, the most important thing to master is the economics of compute. My take: respect the GPU or the GPU will humble you.

We're in a compute shortage. A GB300 costs roughly $7/hour on the spot market so depending on the frontier model, that hour buys you some millions of output tokens.

The only question is: how much customer value can you create with those tokens?

If it's less than $7, you have a problem. Customer won't pay you, so you won't be able to afford more compute, and VCs can subsidize you forever. Eventually, someone who creates more value per GPU-hour will outbid you.

The same GPU-hour could be spent generating another meme or helping discover a cancer treatment. The economic value of those outputs is wildly different.

My take is that you have to design your entire product around this equation. What's the smallest model that can do the job? Can you batch the work? Run it asynchronously during off-peak hours? Avoid generating tokens you don't need?

Every architecture decision, every feature, every token changes your compute economics. The entire roadmap has to be decided for the compute equation. 

What's hard is that in traditional software eng, you could often treat compute as practically free but the agent era, compute is the most important constraint.

There is a second layer to all this that I have not seen anyone discussing.

His claim that the Rosenbergs were "lined up against the wall" is not actually true.  They were executed by electric chair, a method associated exclusively with state-sanctioned formal executions.

"The Wall", OTOH, is a concept currently having a moment with the assassination-left.  It is associated with lynching, struggle sessions, and rogue military action absent central authority or court proceedings.  Countless election-era retweets of right-wing posts titled simply "wall" are just one example.  I think the mistake (intentional?) is telling - accidentally or not, it is precisely worded for maximum amplification in the current moment by people who know exactly what is being said.

🚨 HBM5 Doubles Bandwidth Without Adding a Single Pin 🚨

HBM5 keeps the same 2048 pins as HBM4E and runs each one nearly 2× faster. Samsung's Hot Chips 2026 presentation shows pin speed going from 14 Gbps on HBM4E to over 28 Gbps on HBM5.

Faster pins are only half the story. To keep each pin fed, everything behind the pins doubles too: DRAM banks, TSVs, and an upgraded PHY on the base die.
Here's how it works, explained as a grocery store 🛒 (1/6)🧵

HBM5 keeps the same 2048 pins as HBM4E and runs each one nearly 2× faster. Samsung's Hot Chips 2026 presentation shows pin speed going from 14 Gbps on HBM4E to over 28 Gbps on HBM5.

Faster pins are only half the story. To keep each pin fed, everything behind the pins doubles too: DRAM banks, TSVs, and an upgraded PHY on the base die.
Here's how it works, explained as a grocery store 🛒 (1/6)🧵

Step 2: More data requires more lanes to move it, so the TSVs, which carry data and power up and down the stack, double as well. (4/6) https://t.co/L5w4laZvLK

Step 1: DRAM banks cannot work 2x faster, so HBM5 adds more of them. We estimate 2x the banks per DRAM layer to get there. (3/6) https://t.co/jzxorBRI1c

HBM4 already doubled the number of pins from 1024 to 2048. The GPU's shoreline has limited additional space, so HBM5 keeps the same number of pins and makes each one faster to improve bandwidth. (2/6) https://t.co/mcGMmqYqVS

The catch: HBM5's PHY can run at more than 4x the power of HBM4E. To draw heat off the hot spot, suppliers are introducing a thermal "chimney" placed on top of the PHY.
We cover HBM bandwidth, cost and bit supply in our Memory Model and in "All About That Base: Custom HBM and the New Memory Economics" Subscribe to learn more! 
https://t.co/jGrJoiNm7Z (6/6)

Step 3: The HBM PHY which drives the pins must also run twice as fast to get the data out. In HBM5 it moves to the edge of the base die, cutting the path to the GPU from ~5.5mm to ~2mm per Samsung. Same pins, ~2x the bandwidth. (5/6) https://t.co/Nn6qJQRDhH
